Chapter Nine: Duty and Moral Motivation—The Role of Respect.
Let’s get back to the heart of what really drives us to do the right thing, especially when it’s tough. What actually motivates us to act from a sense of duty? The answer comes down to something pretty special—a feeling called respect for the moral law.
Now, respect isn’t about fear. And it’s not just admiration, either. It’s more like this deep sense of awe you feel when you recognize the demands of reason. It’s that moment when you realize there’s something greater than your own wants—a law that doesn’t command you by force, but by its own rational authority.
Respect for the moral law has a few key features.
First, it’s what I’d call a moral pull. It draws you toward what’s right, even if that choice isn’t easy.
Second, there’s humility. Respect reminds us of our own limits, and of the need to look beyond self-interest.
And finally, respect is empowering. It affirms that you can choose freely, letting reason guide your actions.
Let’s make this real for a second. Imagine finding a wallet stuffed with cash on the street. The temptation to keep it? Yeah, it’s strong. But then this thought pops in: “It would be wrong to take what isn’t mine.” That little voice carries a weight that’s hard to shake—and that, right there, is respect for the moral law coming alive.
So, how can you nurture this kind of motivation in your own life?
Start with some regular self-reflection. Just ask yourself, “What does duty require here?”
Pay attention to your moral feelings. Notice when you feel that sense of respect—or even discomfort—when facing a tough choice.
And don’t forget to celebrate the effort. When you choose duty over what’s easy, give yourself credit for that.
Here’s the real takeaway: Respect for the moral law isn’t just a guide—it’s a source of strength. It helps you do the right thing, not because you’re afraid of consequences or hoping for a reward, but because you care about what’s genuinely good.
